title: Workplace connection has a strong ROI
author: Bruce Daisley
summary: Bruce Daisley's newsletter issue leads with an analysis of KPMG's Friends at Work research, arguing that workplace friendships deliver measurable returns in engagement, skill development, trust and AI adoption. His distinctive move is to add a cautionary note: strong connection amplifies all workplace emotions, so teams with close bonds also report more stress and sadness when job cuts arrive. Daisley reads this as group identity in action and argues that employers cannot take the productivity and loyalty gains while ignoring the emotional intensity that comes with them. The issue then offers short commentary on related reads, including research framing quiet quitting as detachment rather than burnout, Rory Sutherland's claim that technology has turned business into a single-player game, an MIT assessment of how AI is eroding student study groups and confidence, and a United Airlines CEO's cap on meeting time. It closes with a conversation with economist Daniel Susskind, who argues that preparing for advanced AI means shifting education toward cultivating character.
points: KPMG's data show 49% of highly connected workers report being always engaged, and 67% cite a culture of close friendships as a reason to stay with their employer.
Daisley stresses that connected teams also report the highest stress (63%) and sadness (47%) during periods of job cuts, so connection is a package deal.
Workers with close friends at work were far more focused on skill development (87% versus 52%) and more likely to use AI tools.
A linked study reframes quiet quitting as detachment from unfulfilling work rather than burnout, with no quick managerial fix.
Daniel Susskind argues that advanced AI should shift education from workplace competence toward personal character.
quotes: But a new report from KPMG is a powerful indicator that workplace bonds dial up the emotions on all aspects of work - including the stress.
A workplace with strong employee connections is going to find job cuts significantly more emotional that those where workers don’t fraternise together.
This is about group identity in action, when we feel part of something and see colleagues as mattering to us, we become more committed to the job in hand.

Workplace connection is an antidote to burnout and an engine of AI adoption, but it comes as part of a package. We can’t take the productivity gains, the increased loyalty and effort, but then be frustrated when connection amplifies the stress of job cuts and stress.
Worryingly for leaders seeking a fix, the researchers suggest that managers won’t find easy answers to quiet quitting, the trend reflects a broader disaffection with work and society.
Study groups are vanishing, written assignments no longer discriminate between students, the use of chatbots over conversation is killing confidence and connection.
